Richard spent his reign focused on protecting his possessions in France and fighting in the Third Crusade; his brother, John, inherited England in 1199 but lost Normandy and most of Aquitaine after several years of war with France. John fought successive, increasingly expensive, campaigns in a bid to regain these possessions. John's efforts to raise revenues, combined with his fractious relationships with many of the English barons, led to confrontation in 1215, an attempt to restore peace through the signing of the Magna Carta, and finally the outbreak of the First Barons' War. John died having fought the rebel barons and their French backers to a stalemate, and royal power was re-established by barons loyal to the young Henry III. England's power structures remained unstable and the outbreak of the Second Barons' War in 1264 resulted in the king's capture by Simon de Montfort. Henry's son, Edward, defeated the rebel factions between 1265 and 1267, restoring his father to power.

Sir William Maule was the eldest son of Sir Peter Maule and Christina de Valognes, Baron and Baroness of Panmure and Benvie. William succeeded as Baron in 1254 on his father's death. He was married to Ethana de Vallibus, daughter of John Vaux, Lord of Dirleton, and left one son, Henry Maule, who succeeded him as Baron.

Edward Stafford, 3rd Baron Stafford (7 January 1535 – 18 October 1603) was the second surviving son of Henry Stafford, 1st Baron Stafford and Ursula Pole, the younger brother of Henry Stafford, 2nd Baron Stafford. He served in Parliament for Stafford and succeeded his brother to the barony in 1566.

Edward Pellew, 3rd Viscount Exmouth (14 February 1811 – 11 February 1876), was a British peer who inherited the title of Viscount Exmouth from his father and held the title for 42 years. He was the grandson of Edward Pellew, 1st Viscount Exmouth.

Benjamin Stillingfleet was born in Wood Norton, Norfolk, in 1702 to Mary Ann and Edward Stillingfleet, a physician. He was one of four children, and the only son. His grandfather, a bishop, had died in 1699, but left no money to Benjamin's father as he disapproved of his father's opinions and his marriage.
The Painter's Honeymoon is a painting by Frederic Leighton, 1st Baron Leighton, produced and currently housed at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
Angelīna Kučvaļska was born on 6 December 1998 in Saldus, Latvia. Her father died when she was 12 years old. She is a student at Riga 1st secondary school.

Profumo was born in London, the son of former British government minister John Profumo and his wife, actress Valerie Hobson. The Profumo family is of Italian origin. David Profumo would have succeeded his father as 6th Baron Profumo in the nobility of the Kingdom of Sardinia, if the nobility of Italy had not been legally abolished after WW2. In postcolonial Africa, "father of the nation" was a title used by many leaders both to refer to their role in the independence movement as a source of legitimacy, and to use paternalist symbolism as a source of continued popularity. On Joseph Stalin's seventieth birthday in 1949, he was bestowed with the title "Father of Nations" for his establishment of "people's democracies" in countries occupied by the USSR after World War II.The title "Father of the Nation" is sometimes politically contested. A motion in the Parliament of Slovakia to proclaim controversial pre-war leader Andrej Hlinka "father of the nation" barely failed in September 2007.

Edward George Dannreuther (4 November 1844, Strasbourg – 12 February 1905, Hastings) was a German pianist and writer on music, resident from 1863 in England. Young Edward, under pressure from his father to enter banking as a career, a prospect he found uncongenial, escaped to Leipzig in 1859.

Cyprus Popular Bank, known as Marfin Popular Bank from 2006 to 2011, was the second largest banking group in Cyprus until it was 'shuttered' in March 2013. Each state and major mainland territory in Australia has its own parliament: unicameral in the Northern Territory, the ACT, and Queensland; bicameral in other states. Lower houses are called Legislative Assembly (House of Assembly in South Australia and Tasmania), and upper houses are Legislative Council. The Premier heads the government in each state, while the Chief Minister leads in each territory. The Queen is represented by a governor in each state and by the Administrator in the Northern Territory.

Child labour is prevalent in various regions, with significant cultural and economic influences. In Southeast Asia, practices like Mui Tsai were rationalized as cultural traditions, while the Dutch East India Company justified child labour abuses as protective measures. Christian mission schools in Africa required child labour for religious education. Gender roles affect child labour, with girls often performing more domestic work than boys, leading to risks of exploitation. In Australia, child convicts worked from 1888, but child labour was less severe than in Britain due to lower population and agricultural productivity. The ILO's Worst Forms Convention 182 (C182) of 1999, ratified by 151 countries, prohibits severe forms of child labour, including slavery and hazardous work. In 2010, Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest child labour rates, with over 50% of children aged 5-14 working, primarily in agriculture. India contributes to a significant portion of global child labour, prompting government actions to reduce it. Research by Biggeri and Mehrotra highlights macroeconomic factors driving child labour in five Asian nations. Child labour constitutes 22% of Asia's workforce, 32% in Africa, and 17% in Latin America, with Africa having over 65 million child labourers and Asia about 114 million. Brazil has a long history of child labour since its colonization in 1550, but documentation is scarce.
